# Supply Chain Pulse: Components at San Jose Are the Main Problem

**San Jose HQ component shortages drive most of the delay cost.** Network OTIF is 71.7%, and 119 late orders cost $4.40M. San Jose HQ accounts for 73% of that cost ($3.23M) and 83 of the 119 late orders. Component shortage is the leading cause: 67 orders and $2.73M, or 62% of late cost.

## Evidence

| Plant | OTIF | Late cost | Material loss | Worst component (shortfall) | Riskiest tool (fail prob) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| San Jose HQ | 59.7% | $3,233,345 | 47.9 | Vision Camera Module (50.7 d) | DEPO-1 (3.5%) |
| Dresden Fab | 82.3% | $423,050 | 9.3 | Reflectance Detector Array (38.9 d) | LIT3-2 (3.3%) |
| Austin Fab | 81.3% | $385,930 | 21.4 | Vacuum Chamber (38.9 d) | **Stepper LIT2-1 (50.6%)** |
| Penang Assembly | 79.5% | $351,920 | 14.7 | UV Laser Module (20.4 d) | PKG5-1 (3.0%) |
| Singapore Hub | 96.3% | $10,500 | 6.7 | Wafer Handler (39.7 d) | **ASM4-1 (35.0%)** |

**Why it matters:**
- **Components bind everywhere.** All five plants list Components as their binding constraint.
- **San Jose's camera supply will not recover soon.** It has 5.3 days of cover for the Vision Camera Module against a 56-day lead time from Coherent Corp.
- **Quality exposure is wide.** 18 of 107 lots are deviating, which puts 161 orders and $132.4M of value at risk.
  - TRUMPF lot CL-201-04 (Vacuum Chamber) alone reached 28 systems across 6 customers.
- **Sourcing is fragile.** Six categories are single-source.

**Relationships followed:**
- System Serial -has part-> Component Lot
- System Serial -shipped on-> Sales Order -placed by-> Customer
- Plant -operates-> Tool for equipment risk

## Actions

1. **Expedite the Vision Camera Module now.** Ask Coherent Corp to expedite or split shipments, and qualify an alternate source. Then run the "Shortage — Vision Camera Module" preset (35% severity, 50 days) to re-plan San Jose commitments.
2. **Do preventive maintenance on Stepper LIT2-1 in Austin within 48 hours.** It has a 51% failure risk and anomalous vibration, and its work center is about 30% of the plant's capacity. Schedule ASM4-1 in Singapore next.
3. **Contain CL-201-04.** Place the TRUMPF hold (SUP-004, 21 days). Trace the 28 affected systems to their sales orders and customers, and notify those 6 customers proactively.
4. **Start dual-sourcing** for the six single-source categories, prioritizing those feeding San Jose.

# Deviating Component Lots: Analysis

**The main finding:** 18 of 107 component lots are deviating, and they reach **161 sales orders worth $132.4M**. Two problems stand out:

- **Rejected lots were still built into systems.** Five lots inspected as *Rejected* went into 77 systems.
- **Deviating lots fail far more often at final test.** They have much higher not-first-pass rates than clean lots.

**Path followed:** System Serial -has part-> Component Lot -supplied by-> Supplier. Exposure comes from System Serial -shipped on-> Sales Order -placed by-> Customer, and plants from System Serial -built at-> Plant.

| Lot | Supplier | Inspection | Systems | Not first pass | Order value |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| CL-103-04 | Festo AG | Accepted w/ deviation | 19 | 6 (32%) | $18.1M |
| CL-402-07 | Hamamatsu | Accepted w/ deviation | 29 | 12 (41%) | $16.4M |
| CL-201-04 | TRUMPF | **Rejected** | 28 | 10 (36%) | $16.4M |
| CL-700-03 | Coherent | Accepted w/ deviation | 39 | 19 (49%) | $15.5M |
| CL-300-07 | TRUMPF | **Rejected** | 20 | 7 (35%) | $11.8M |
| CL-701-04 | Aerotech | Accepted | 27 | 14 (52%) | $12.5M |
| CL-103-06 (baseline) | Festo AG | Accepted | 31 | 1 (3%) | $28.5M |

**Why it matters**

- **Inspection may not be blocking material.** Rejected lots appear in shipped serials. This points to a gap in quality holds or an undocumented use-as-is decision.
- **Some suppliers repeat.** Festo has 5 deviating lots, TRUMPF and Coherent have 4 each, and both TRUMPF lots were rejected.
- **Problems compound in some serials.** 19 serials carry two deviating lots, 11 of them MAT-1004. Three of these failed final test (SN-1001-02860 and SN-1004-01271 for Intel Fab, SN-1002-03200 for Texas Instruments).
- **A possible hidden escape.** CL-701-04 passed inspection, yet 52% of its systems did not pass first time.

**Actions**

1. **Audit how the five rejected lots were released.** Confirm whether material review board (MRB) approvals exist, and enforce a hard block in SAP.
2. **Prioritise outreach to customers on double-exposed serials,** starting with Intel Fab and Texas Instruments. Plan field service for CL-700-03 and CL-402-07 systems.
3. **Issue supplier corrective action requests (SCARs)** to TRUMPF (vacuum chamber and UV laser) and Festo (control cabinet), and tighten incoming inspection for both.
4. **Re-inspect CL-701-04 and quarantine any remaining stock** until the cause is found.

*Note:* this is demo enrichment data, and the lot counts differ between sources (107 in the KPIs vs 114 instances).

# Equipment Risk Analysis: Two Outliers Need Action

**Two tools stand far apart from the rest of the fleet. Stepper LIT2-1 (Austin) is the urgent one. Robotic Assembly Cell ASM4-1 (Singapore) is a hidden risk because it is not flagged.**

## What stands out

| Equipment | Plant | Criticality | Failure prob. (48h) | Vibration (mm/s) | Anomaly flag | Plant open orders |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Stepper LIT2-1 | Austin Fab | B | **50.55%** | **4.866** | **TRUE** | 1 (of 64, $54.59M) |
| Robotic Assembly Cell ASM4-1 | Singapore Hub | B | **34.97%** | **4.157** | false | 0 (of 27, $22.62M) |
| Next highest (CVD DEPO-1, PVD DEP2-2) | San Jose / Austin | B / C | 3.47% | 1.721 / 1.286 | false | n/a |
| Highest of the remaining 16 tools | n/a | n/a | ≤3.40% | ≤2.182 | false | n/a |

## Why it matters

- **LIT2-1 is roughly 15× riskier than the next tool** outside the top two. Its vibration is more than double the rest of the fleet. It is the only Stepper at Austin in this data; Austin's other Lithography tool, Track LIT2-2, is criticality A. A stepper outage would stall Austin lithography while the plant has an open order.
- **ASM4-1 is high-risk but unflagged.** At 34.97% probability and 4.157 mm/s, it has no anomaly flag. This points to a gap in anomaly-flag logic or thresholds. It is also the only assembly cell at Singapore in this data.
- All readings are dated 2025-09-30. The 48-hour window may already be stale, so confirm with current telemetry.

## Actions

1. **Austin:** Schedule immediate inspection or maintenance on LIT2-1. Check whether wafers can be rerouted to Stepper LITHO-1 (San Jose, 3.32%) or Stepper LIT3-1 (Dresden, 2.69%) to protect the open order.
2. **Singapore:** Inspect ASM4-1 now. Singapore has no open orders, so this is a low-cost maintenance window. Keep Penang's ASM5-1 (2.7%) as overflow capacity.
3. **Anomaly logic:** Review the rules behind the flag. A tool at 35% failure probability and above 4 mm/s should trigger it.
4. **Data freshness:** Pull post-September 30 readings for both tools before committing production schedules.

**Relationships followed:** Equipment -located at-> Plant; Plant -fulfills-> Sales Order (order counts, value and open orders).

# San Jose HQ's component supply is the network's biggest weakness

**San Jose HQ is short on components, and single-source categories leave no fallback.** San Jose handles 49% of orders (206 of 420) but carries 73% of late cost ($3.23M of $4.40M), with OTIF at 59.7%. Component shortage is the leading late cause network-wide: 67 orders and $2.73M, or 62% of late cost.

| Scenario | Value at risk | % network | Protected by reroute |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hurricane, Austin offline | $16.05M | 28.3% | 91.4% |
| **Vision Camera Module shortage, San Jose** | **$13.90M** | **24.5%** | **39.9% ($7.37M unprotected)** |
| Hamamatsu supplier failure | $9.08M | 16.0% | 70.2% |
| Typhoon, Penang offline | $5.85M | 10.3% | **0%** |
| Stepper LIT2-1 failure, Austin | $1.03M | 1.8% | 100% |

**Why**

- **Vision Camera Module is the most likely and least recoverable disruption.** San Jose has 5.3 days of cover against a 56-day lead time from Coherent Corp, with a worst shortfall of 50.7 days. It impairs Penang and Singapore two hops out.
- **Missing categories block rerouting.** The governed definition (Snowflake Business Ontology) of Material Category says sole-source risk "is a property of a category, not of a plant." The six single-source categories confirm it. "Die Sorting: no alternative plant makes this category" appears in five scenarios, and Surface Analysis and E-Beam Review are also stranded.
- **Tool risk is real but contained.** Stepper LIT2-1 has a 50.6% failure probability, but its revenue is fully reroutable to San Jose.

**Relationships followed:**

- Plant -produces-> Material Category -CLASSIFIES-> Material Flow
- Sales Order -fulfilled by-> Plant
- Sales Order -placed by-> Customer
- System Serial -HAS_PART-> Component Lot -supplied by-> Supplier
- Equipment -installed at-> Plant

**Actions**

1. **Expedite Vision Camera Module now.** Pursue air freight or spot buys from Coherent, and start qualifying a second source. The 56-day lead time far exceeds the 5.3 days of cover.
2. **Qualify a second plant for Die Sorting and Surface Analysis.** These are the categories that cannot reroute in most scenarios. Penang's 0% protection under a typhoon depends on this.
3. **Schedule preventive maintenance on Stepper LIT2-1 (Austin) and ASM4-1 (Singapore).** Their failure probabilities are 51% and 35%. Pre-book San Jose reroute capacity for GlobalFoundries and Micron.
4. **Contain TRUMPF lot CL-201-04.** This rejected lot reached 28 systems across 6 customers. Trace it via System Serial -HAS_PART-> Component Lot before the hold widens.

**Governed definition (Snowflake Business Ontology):** a Plant is *a manufacturing site* and *a kind of Facility* (Plant -IS_A-> Facility). Capacity (work centres, hours, spare units) and inventory (days of cover, stock value) are modelled as **properties of the Plant**, not as separate entities, because each is 1:1 with the plant. Facility is abstract, so distribution centres or contract manufacturers could be added later as the same kind of thing.

**How the app uses Plant.** It is the hub of the model. Governed relationships followed:

- Equipment -installed at-> Plant
- System Serial -built at-> Plant
- Sales Order -fulfilled by-> Plant
- Supplier -supplies-> Plant
- Plant -ships to-> Customer
- Plant -produces-> Material Category

The app uses these relationships in two ways:

1. **Plant scorecards** roll up orders, OTIF, late cost, tool risk and component shortfall.
2. **Disruption scenarios** treat plants as impaired nodes and as reroute targets.

# Serial SN-1001-01031: Analysis

**A rejected component lot appears to be built into a shipped, customer-installed system.** SN-1001-01031 (KLA 8935 Wafer Inspection System, Austin Fab) passed final test with 0 rework hours. It shipped on time (OTIF) to Infineon Technologies on SO-4500103 ($1,296,000). However, 2 of its 4 component lots carry deviations, and one was **Rejected** at incoming inspection.

**Relationships followed:** System Serial -has part-> Component Lot -supplied by-> Supplier; System Serial -shipped on-> Sales Order -placed by-> Customer; System Serial -built at-> Plant.

| Lot | Supplier | Component | Result | Note | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| CL-102-01 | Aerotech Inc | Precision Motion Stage | **Rejected** | Vacuum seal leak rate high | SAP |
| CL-103-04 | Festo AG | Control Electronics Cabinet | Accepted with deviation | Surface contamination on optics | DEMO |
| CL-100-02 | Hamamatsu Photonics | Broadband Light Source | Accepted | none | SAP |
| CL-101-03 | Teledyne DALSA | High-Res CCD Array | Accepted | none | SAP |

**Why it matters**
- **Rejected lot in a shipped unit.** A rejected lot should not be consumed. Either it was released by a waiver that the facts don't show, or the lot linkage is wrong. A vacuum leak in the motion stage is a field-reliability risk that final test may not catch.
- **Zero rework despite a rejected part.** This suggests no replacement or repair was recorded.
- **Data inconsistency on CL-103-04.** "Contamination on optics" doesn't fit a control electronics cabinet. The record is demo-sourced, not SAP, so treat it as lower confidence.
- **Exposure is concentrated.** This is a strategic customer and a $1.3M system, and on-time performance masked the quality issue.

**Actions**
1. **Verify the CL-102-01 disposition** in SAP QM, including any usage decision or waiver. If none exists, open a containment and notify Infineon field service for a proactive vacuum-seal check.
2. **Trace all serials that consumed CL-102-01** (7 units) and CL-103-04 (28 units) for wider exposure.
3. **Raise a SCAR with Aerotech** on seal leak rate, and audit Austin's goods-issue controls that allowed a rejected lot through.
4. **Correct or confirm the CL-103-04 record** and its component mapping before relying on it.

# Lot CL-103-04: Control Electronics Cabinet (Festo AG)

**Direct answer:** This lot was **accepted with deviation**, and **6 of the 19 systems (32%)** built with it did not pass first time. Those systems feed **14 sales orders worth $18.14M** across **6 major fab customers**. A known-deviation lot with weak first-pass performance and broad customer exposure is the main risk here.

## Evidence

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Component | Control Electronics Cabinet |
| Supplier | Festo AG |
| Inspection result | Accepted with deviation |
| Systems using lot | 19 |
| Systems not first-pass | 6 (≈32%) |
| Sales orders | 14 |
| Customers | 6 (GlobalFoundries, Infineon, Intel Fab, Micron, Samsung, TI) |
| Order value | $18,144,000 |

## Why it matters

- **Deviation and failures.** The lot entered production with a documented deviation, and nearly a third of the systems using it failed first pass. That points to the deviation as a likely cause. The facts don't include the deviation details or a baseline first-pass rate, so this still needs to be confirmed.
- **High-impact part.** The control electronics cabinet is central to each system, so a latent defect could show up in the field.
- **Wide exposure.** The lot reaches six of the largest semiconductor manufacturers, so the reputational and revenue risk goes beyond the $18.1M directly tied to it.

## Relationships followed

- System Serial -has part-> Component Lot (CL-103-04)
- Component Lot → Supplier (Festo AG)
- System Serial -shipped on-> Sales Order -placed by-> Customer

## Recommended actions

1. **Contain:** Flag all 19 system serials. Hold any that haven't shipped, and prioritise retest or rework of the 6 that failed first pass.
2. **Root cause:** Pull the deviation record and compare the failure modes of the 6 systems against it. Open a formal corrective action (8D) with Festo AG.
3. **Customer risk:** Map the 14 orders to install status. Prepare proactive service or field-inspection plans, starting with the largest-value orders.
4. **Policy:** Tighten "accept with deviation" approvals for control electronics, and check other Festo lots for the same deviation.

**Direct answer:** Dresden's 30-day drop to 60% puts **$3.76M revenue at risk** (7.3% of monthly network value). The reroute plan protects **only 44.7% ($1.68M)**. The rest is **Infineon's E-Beam Review flow (FL-018, $2.08M)**, which cannot be moved because no other plant makes that category.

There is also a hidden risk the headline numbers miss. Dresden's 35-day buffer covers the 30-day event, so the model shows 0 plants impaired and 0 orders at risk. But the plant's binding constraint is **Components**, and the **Reflectance Detector Array** has a 38.9-day shortfall. That is longer than the buffer, and the model does not trace it because the multi-level BOM is not exploded.

**Evidence**

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Cost of disruption | $541,765 ($494,325 lost margin + $47,440 late penalty) |
| FL-019 Samsung → San Jose HQ | $1.68M protected; 49.2 of 282 hrs used; headroom 9% after; +892 km |
| FL-018 Infineon (E-Beam Review) | $2.08M unmitigable, single-source |
| Dresden baseline | 82.3% OTIF; 14 late orders ($423,050 late cost); 9.3 material loss vs 2.5 equipment loss |
| Worst component | Reflectance Detector Array: 38.9-day shortfall vs 35-day buffer |
| Riskiest tool | Track LIT3-2: failure probability 0.033; 0 tools at risk |

Dresden was already underperforming before this event. Its 82.3% OTIF and its material losses (much higher than equipment losses) point to components, not tools, as the weak link.

**Relationships followed:** Plant -ships-> Flow -serves-> Customer; Plant -operates-> Tool; Plant -consumes-> Component Lot.

**Actions**
1. **Execute the FL-019 reroute now.** San Jose will have only 9% headroom left, so freeze other new loads there for the 30 days.
2. **Protect the Infineon flow at Dresden.** Give FL-018 priority on the remaining 60% capacity and agree a revised delivery schedule with Infineon early. This targets the $2.08M exposure.
3. **Expedite or second-source the Reflectance Detector Array.** Its shortfall outlasts the buffer, so it could turn a "covered" event into real late orders.
4. **Add capability to make the E-Beam Review category at a second plant.** This removes the single point of failure for future events.

# Scenario: San Jose → Penang lane closed for 40 days

**Direct answer:** This closure puts **$3.73M of value at risk (6.6% of monthly network value)** and costs an estimated **$298K** ($272K lost margin plus $26K late penalties). Nearly all the exposure lands on two customers, **TSMC and Texas Instruments**, through one plant: **Penang Assembly**.

## What stands out

1. **One lane, two key customers.** FL-025 carries San Jose sub-assemblies, about 34.5% of Penang's inbound volume. Penang's 12-day buffer absorbs the first part of the event, leaving **28 days exposed**. That shortfall passes straight to Penang's die-sorting outflows to TSMC and TI.
2. **Penang is already fragile.** Its on-time-in-full (OTIF) rate is 79.5%, with 9 late orders costing $352K. Its binding constraint is Components: the **UV Laser Module** is 20.4 days short. The model does not explode the bill of materials, so the closure and this existing shortage are **not combined**. True impact is likely understated.
3. **"0 orders at risk" is misleading.** Penang holds a **$964K open order**, the largest open order in the network.
4. **The horizons don't match.** Downstream customer flows are scored over 40 days, but Penang is exposed for only 28. Validate this before quoting final numbers.

| Flow | Route | Monthly value | Value at risk | Hop |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FL-022 | Penang → TSMC | $3.60M | $1.66M | 2 |
| FL-025 | San Jose → Penang | $1.60M | $1.05M | 1 (closed) |
| FL-023 | Penang → TI | $2.25M | $1.03M | 2 |

## Actions

1. **Reroute sub-assemblies within the 12-day buffer window.** Use air freight or go through Singapore Hub, which has 96.3% OTIF and no open orders, to restore part of FL-025.
2. **Protect TSMC first** ($1.66M at risk), and secure the $964K open order at Penang ahead of other work.
3. **Expedite the UV Laser Module** so a component shortage doesn't stack on top of the lane loss.
4. **Rerun the scenario with consistent horizons and an exploded BOM**, then confirm the figures before any customer communication.

**Relationships followed:** Plant (San Jose) -ships via-> Flow FL-025 -supplies-> Plant (Penang) -ships via-> Flow FL-022/FL-023 -delivers to-> Customer (TSMC/TI); Plant -has operations-> SC360 metrics.

# TSMC +60% Demand Spike: Analysis

**Direct answer:** This is an upside scenario, not a supply failure. A 30-day, +60% TSMC demand spike creates **$8.82M of revenue at risk**, 15.6% of monthly network value. It costs nothing only if we can fulfil it. No plants are impaired and cost of disruption is $0. The real risk is capacity: **San Jose HQ carries 57% of the extra demand but has the worst OTIF in the network (59.7%).**

## Evidence

I followed the outbound flow relationships Plant → Flow → Customer (CUS-001 TSMC), then joined plant-level order economics. All three affected flows are at hop 1.

| Flow | Source plant | Category | Extra units / 30d | Value at risk | Plant OTIF | Plant open orders |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FL-013 | San Jose HQ | Inspection Systems | 2.4 (on 4) | $5.04M | **59.7%** | 1 / $338K |
| FL-022 | Penang Assembly | Die Sorting | 4.8 (on 8) | $2.16M | 79.5% | 1 / $964K |
| FL-020 | Singapore Hub | Surface Analysis | 1.8 (on 3) | $1.62M | 96.3% | 0 |

## Why it matters

- **San Jose is the bottleneck.** Its TSMC flow is $8.4M/month, equivalent to about 53% of San Jose's $15.96M monthly order value. San Jose already misses roughly 40% of its OTIF commitments, so adding 60% more demand on its biggest customer flow risks both the new revenue and service on existing orders.
- **Cost of disruption may be understated.** The $0 figure reflects the model treating this as demand rather than lost supply. The model does not explode the multi-level BOM, so component-lot shortages inside San Jose or Penang are not traced and could block fulfilment.
- **Singapore has headroom.** It has 96.3% OTIF and no open backlog, so it is low risk.

## Actions

1. **Run a San Jose capacity and component check.** Explode the Inspection Systems BOM to see whether component lots support about 6 systems/month instead of 4, and expedite any long-lead parts now.
2. **Protect Penang's backlog.** Sequence the $964K open order against the extra 4.8 Die Sorting units so existing commitments are not cannibalised.
3. **Confirm the spike with TSMC.** Verify whether the 30-day horizon is firm, then agree phased delivery dates rather than promising full volume from San Jose at current OTIF.
4. **Price the upside.** Model the margin at 52.1%: if fully captured, the spike is worth about $4.6M of margin. That justifies overtime or expedite spend at San Jose.

# TSMC +60% Demand Spike: $8.82M Opportunity at Risk with No Mitigation Plan

**The scenario puts $8.82M of revenue at risk (15.6% of the $56.69M monthly network value), but the mitigation plan protects $0.** That is a modelling blind spot, not a sign that everything is fine.

## What stands out

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Revenue at risk | $8,820,000 |
| Share of network | 15.6% |
| Customers affected | 1 (TSMC, CUS-001) |
| Plants impaired | 0 |
| Orders at risk / cost of disruption | 0 / $0 |
| Reroutes planned | None (3 plants considered, 0% protected) |
| Max hop | 1 |

## Why

This is a **demand-side** event, but the propagation model is built for **supply loss**. It spreads impact by each node's dependence on lost inbound flow. Extra demand removes no flow, so:

- The walk stopped at the origin (hop 0). It went no further than Sales Order -placed by-> Customer (TSMC).
- No plant was flagged as impaired, so the planner had nothing to reroute.
- Cost of disruption shows $0 because no lost output was modelled.

The real risk is that we **cannot fulfil** the extra 60% for 30 days. That depends on plant capacity and component availability, which this run does not test. The multi-level BOM is also not exploded, so shortages inside a plant are invisible.

## Recommended actions

1. **Check capacity.** Identify which plants build TSMC's systems (Sales Order → Plant). Confirm whether they can absorb +60% for 30 days, including the 12-day-type inventory buffers.
2. **Explode the BOM for TSMC configurations.** Use System Serial -has part-> Component Lot to find long-lead or single-source components that would cap output.
3. **Re-run as a supply constraint.** Model the binding plant or component limits, then let the planner allocate across the 3 available plants. This gives a real protected-versus-unprotected split.
4. **Agree allocation and timing with TSMC.** Confirm firm versus forecast volume. Phase delivery so other customers' orders aren't cannibalised.
